title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by the fallout from the US midterms, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress. President Trump named Stephen Miller as chief of staff, and AI and tech stocks swung sharply amid expectations of tougher scrutiny of AI. Abroad, Paraguay's president was impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse. Other stories include a faculty no-confidence vote at Cornell, a rejected wage deal at POSCO, North Korea–China party talks, and Charlotte-area local news.

stories.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles after midterm losses
stories.summary: President Trump announced Friday that Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff starting Monday, November 9. The move came three days after Democrats won majorities in both the House and Senate. Trump praised Wiles and said she will move to the "Trump Political Operation"; she reportedly submitted her resignation Thursday night. Democratic leaders condemned the pick, and several outlets and commentators read it as a sign that Trump will double down on hardline policies rather than moderate. Trump has not announced any further staff changes.
key_facts: Miller, 41, takes over as chief of staff on Monday, November 9, 2026.
Wiles was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff and had held the job since January 2025.
Trump said: "I wanted to make a change... Stephen's been great, and we've got to make moves."
Hakeem Jeffries called Miller "a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist" and said "Fire him today."
Miller is widely described as the architect of the administration's immigration crackdown.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and PBS called Miller the "most controversial" and "polarizing" aide and said Wiles was "ousted." They foregrounded condemnations from Jeffries and Schumer and commentators who called the move "a declaration of war." They tied the pick to immigration becoming a political liability. PBS widened the story to Republican infighting, including criticism over the Iran war and Defense Secretary Hegseth.

Axios framed the move as Trump trading "one of his few moderating forces" for a maximalist, driven by anger over the midterm losses, and reported that sources called the departure mutual. The Hill led with Jeffries's attack. The Korea Herald/Yonhap took a more neutral, announcement-focused approach and highlighted Wiles's role as a channel to South Korea.

Reason, a libertarian outlet, published an opinion piece arguing that Miller will "reinforce Trump's worst instincts." It criticised his record on immigration, habeas corpus, birthright citizenship, courts and free speech, and argued the pick dims hopes of moderation after the midterms.

disputed: Whether Wiles left by mutual decision (Axios sources) or was pushed out (Guardian's word was "ousted").
Whether more personnel changes will follow; Trump has announced none.
Whether the appointment signals confrontation with the new Democratic Congress. Commentators say it does; Trump had pledged to work with Congress, according to PBS.
stories.why: The chief of staff shapes how the White House operates, and this pick signals how Trump may approach a Democratic-controlled Congress.

stories.headline: Paraguay's Senate removes President Santiago Peña, who is placed under house arrest after Ueno bank collapse
stories.summary: Paraguay's Senate voted Friday to remove President Santiago Peña for misconduct after the collapse of Ueno, a digital bank with ties to him. The collapse froze accounts for roughly 2.9 million customers. Senators impeached him instead of accepting his resignation, which stripped him of the immunity and lifetime Senate seat granted to ex-presidents. Prosecutors then ordered his arrest, along with former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, and Peña was placed under house arrest pending questioning on Saturday. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in to serve until August 2028. Peña denies wrongdoing, and his lawyer called the accusations "reckless" and "opportunistic."
key_facts: All 44 senators present voted to remove Peña; BBC said one of 45 was absent.
Ueno served about 2.94 million customers, roughly 60% of Paraguay's adults.
The central bank ordered Ueno's resolution or closure on Tuesday after its solvency ratio fell below half the required minimum.
Peña held shares in Ueno's parent company until April 2025 and named Carvallo, Ueno's former head, as central bank chief in 2023.
Peña is to be questioned Saturday on allegations including breach of trust and influence peddling.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian called Peña a "rightwing president" and one of Trump's main allies in the region. It emphasised alleged favouritism toward Ueno and the conflict of interest in Carvallo regulating his former company, and quoted an analyst on pension funds flowing to the bank. Al Jazeera reported that Peña was moved to a military base for his own protection.

DW and BBC gave detailed, procedural accounts: the impeachment articles, the resignation manoeuvre, public-fund exposure and protests. BBC included Peña's denial, his lawyer's response, Alliana's pledge to compensate depositors, and a senator calling it the biggest corruption scandal in the country's democratic history.

The New York Post (via wire reporting) highlighted celebrating crowds, depositors' anger and the possible 10-year prison terms. It noted that Peña is the second president impeached since the Stroessner dictatorship and reported that Alliana is himself under investigation in connection with the bank.

disputed: The exact charges are described differently across outlets: illicit enrichment and money laundering (Guardian), versus breach of trust, influence peddling and misuse of office (BBC, NY Post).
Whether Peña formally resigned (DW) or only attempted to, with lawmakers refusing to accept it (Guardian, BBC).
Al Jazeera reports Peña was moved to a military base; other outlets describe house arrest at his home.
Whether Carvallo was taken into custody.
Whether and how depositors will be repaid.
The extent of Alliana's own investigation.
stories.why: A bank failure locking most adults out of their money has toppled a sitting president, testing the stability of Paraguay's institutions and economy.

stories.headline: Cornell faculty senate passes no-confidence vote over handling of sexual assault allegations; trustees back president
stories.summary: Cornell University's Faculty Senate voted 75-50 on Friday to declare no confidence in the administration's ability to address what it called a sexual assault crisis. The vote followed a lawsuit by a former student, known as Jane Doe, who alleges she was drugged and raped at a Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024; the seven accused men deny it. The vote is symbolic because the faculty senate has no power to remove leaders. The board of trustees said the vote reflected deep anger on campus but that it fully supports President Michael Kotlikoff. Kotlikoff has 30 days to respond in writing.
key_facts: The vote was 75-50, with five abstentions and five senators not voting.
The local district attorney initially declined to prosecute; New York's attorney general is now investigating.
Cornell disciplined students after a Title IX investigation: two were expelled, two suspended, and two assigned reflection papers.
The resolution did not call for Kotlikoff's resignation.
Governor Hochul said state police would investigate future sexual offence complaints at the university.

perspectives.framing: PBS and The Guardian (both carrying Associated Press reporting) described the vote as a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent. They detailed the disciplinary outcomes, the district attorney's initial finding of consent, and statements from the trustees and Doe's lawyer.

DW, BBC and The Hill gave similar accounts, adding Kotlikoff's listed reforms and the trustees' support. BBC noted that the resolution made no specific recommendations and reported the dispute over Doe's account of Kotlikoff's reaction to her.

disputed: The underlying allegations are denied by all seven men, and none has been charged.
Doe says Kotlikoff asked why she waited to report; Cornell calls her account "incorrect."
Whether criminal charges will follow from the attorney general's review.
stories.why: The case is a high-profile test of how universities handle sexual assault allegations and who is held accountable.

stories.headline: Expectations for Anthropic's IPO valuation fall as OpenAI raises funds at $1.25 trillion
stories.summary: After this week's tech selloff, investors told CNBC that a $1.5 trillion valuation for Anthropic's upcoming Nasdaq IPO now looks like a "stretch," down from a reported target of as much as $2 trillion. Anthropic declined to comment and is expected to start its roadshow next week. Separately, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI has raised $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, in a round that could reach about $20 billion. That is below its earlier hoped-for $30 billion at $1.4 trillion. Outlets linked the cooling to the market slump and to voter backlash against AI and data centres in the midterms.
key_facts: Anthropic was privately valued at $965 billion as of May and plans to list under the ticker ANT.
OpenAI's new round values it at $1.25 trillion, with $11 billion raised so far.
OpenAI was valued at $852 billion in March, when it raised $122 billion.
The Nasdaq fell more than 5% on Thursday, its steepest drop in 19 months.

perspectives.framing: The Verge focused on OpenAI's raise and tied the lower figures to public opinion turning against AI companies and data centres. It noted Sam Altman's comments about putting safety before an IPO.

CNBC and TechCrunch focused on investor expectations and market conditions, quoting an analyst who said the market "really needs this IPO to go well." They cited anticipated regulatory challenges after the Democratic wins.

disputed: Anthropic's likely valuation: investors told CNBC $1–1.25 trillion, while Bloomberg cited buyers suggesting as low as $1.1 trillion.
Neither company has confirmed the figures; OpenAI's round has not closed.
stories.why: The pricing of the largest AI companies is a key gauge of whether investor enthusiasm for AI is holding up.

stories.headline: Two people seriously injured in shooting near UNC Charlotte
stories.summary: Two people were shot Friday at about 4:15 p.m. at off-campus apartments on Education Way in Charlotte's University City area, near UNC Charlotte. MEDIC said both had life-threatening injuries. WSOC noted that homicide detectives were not called, which it said strongly suggests the victims are expected to survive. No information on victims or suspects has been released.
key_facts: The shooting happened in the 10900 block of Education Way, off East Mallard Creek Church Road.
Two people were taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries, according to MEDIC.

perspectives.framing: Local TV outlets reported the basic facts from MEDIC and described it as a developing story.

disputed: The victims' identities, any suspects and the motive are unknown.
stories.why: It is a serious violent incident in a busy student housing area.

stories.headline: US tech stocks partly rebound after midterm-linked selloff; Asian and European markets fall
stories.summary: The Nasdaq rose about 1% on Friday, recovering part of Thursday's 5.5% drop. That drop was driven by fears that Democrats' midterm wins and voter skepticism of AI would slow data centre expansion. A stronger-than-expected jobs report of 165,000 new jobs helped sentiment. Asian and European markets fell, with South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei down about 6% and the FTSE 100 down about 1%. President Trump reiterated his support for "super intelligence," while analysts warned that more selling could follow.
key_facts: The Nasdaq fell 5.5% on Thursday, its worst day in 19 months.
On Friday the S&P 500 closed up 0.3% and the Dow fell 0.4%.
The FTSE 100 closed down about 1% after falling as much as 2.35% during the day.
SK Hynix shares fell more than 10%.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian stressed the global rout and margin calls, quoting strategists on worries about returns from AI spending and possible renewed Iran conflict. It also noted that most indices are still up for the year.

BBC emphasised the partial recovery and the mixed picture. It quoted voices saying the election signals a need to rethink AI, including one who called the drop a "necessary market correction," and included Trump's pro-AI remarks.

disputed: The jobs report month: BBC says September, while The Guardian says October with unemployment at 4.1%.
Small differences in figures: the Nasdaq's Friday gain (1.1% vs 1%) and the Kospi's drop (6% vs more than 6.5%).
Whether further selling will follow.
stories.why: Expectations about AI regulation under a Democratic Congress are moving global markets and retirement portfolios.

stories.headline: Silfab Solar to restart chemical commissioning at Fort Mill plant
stories.summary: Silfab Solar gave South Carolina environmental regulators a 72-hour notice on Friday that it will restart chemical commissioning at its Fort Mill plant on Monday. The work has been paused since March, after two chemical leaks. The company said it completed a thorough review of the facility and its procedures. It also said the restart does not mean manufacturing will begin immediately.
key_facts: Notice was given to the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services on Friday.
Work had been paused since two chemical leaks in March.
Commissioning restarts Monday.

perspectives.framing: Local outlets relayed the company's announcement, with WSOC noting its months of coverage of the leaks.

disputed: When actual manufacturing will begin.
stories.why: Nearby residents have followed the plant's safety record since the March leaks.

stories.headline: POSCO union members reject tentative wage deal
stories.summary: Unionised workers at South Korean steelmaker POSCO rejected a tentative wage agreement, with 51.69% voting against. The deal, reached October 30 after about 30 rounds of talks, included a 2.6% base pay rise, a 6 million won lump sum and improved benefits. The union had initially sought a 7.1% raise and other bonuses. A union official said renegotiations will likely be needed, and management said it remains committed to dialogue.
key_facts: 51.69% voted against the deal and 48.31% voted for it.
Talks began June 16, and the union held two partial strikes in September.

perspectives.framing: Korea Herald and Yonhap gave straightforward accounts quoting both union and management.

disputed: The timing of renegotiations and whether further strikes will follow.
stories.why: Labour unrest at a major steelmaker could affect South Korean industry.

stories.headline: Senior North Korean official holds third high-level meeting in Beijing
stories.summary: Kim Song-nam, the head of international affairs for North Korea's Workers' Party, met Chinese Communist Party officials Liu Haixing and Cai Qi in Beijing on Friday, according to North Korean state media. The meetings were part of a four-day visit that also included talks with Foreign Minister Wang Yi. Both sides pledged deeper ties, and Cai said China's friendship would not waver regardless of international changes. Yonhap linked the visit to efforts to repair ties after they appeared to cool over North Korea's alignment with Russia.
key_facts: Kim arrived in Beijing on Tuesday for a four-day visit.
The talks follow Xi Jinping's June summit with Kim Jong-un in Pyongyang.

perspectives.framing: Both outlets relied on North Korean state media accounts; Yonhap added context about cooled relations over Russia.

disputed: Accounts come mainly from North Korean state media.
stories.why: Closer China–North Korea ties shape regional security.

stories.headline: Lee marks South Korea's first persimmon export to China in 17 years
stories.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on X that Korean persimmons are entering the Chinese market after 17 years of negotiations. He pledged support for opening new export markets for farmers. In a separate post, he backed Busan's push to become a maritime hub after foreign card spending in the city passed 1 trillion won.
key_facts: This is the first persimmon shipment to China after 17 years of negotiations.
Foreign credit card spending in Busan passed 1 trillion won.

perspectives.framing: The Korea Herald relayed Lee's posts without additional comment.

stories.why: It is a small trade opening that reflects efforts to diversify South Korea's farm exports.

investigations.update: No articles directly address US or EU AI regulation. Market coverage (stories s4 and s6) notes that Democrats campaigned on AI and data centre rules and that investors expect more regulatory scrutiny from the incoming Congress, but no specific legislation or EU action was reported.
